name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q01 - Electrical quantities and their SI units

questiontext.text:
Match the electrical quantities in List I with their corresponding SI units in List II:

List I (Quantity)List II (SI Unit)
(1) Resistance (\(R\))(A) \(\mathrm{S}\)
(2) Conductance (\(G\))(B) \(\mathrm{S\ m^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)
(3) Conductivity (\(\kappa\))(C) \(\Omega\)
(4) Molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{m}\))(D) \(\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrical resistance, conductance, conductivity, and molar conductivity are related through the geometry of the conducting path (\(l\) and \(A\)) and the molar concentration (\(c\)) of the electrolyte.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Quantity and Unit
1. Electrical resistance \(R\) is measured in ohm (\(\Omega\)).
2. Conductance \(G = \frac{1}{R}\) is the inverse of resistance, so its SI unit is siemens (\(\mathrm{S}\)), equal to \(\Omega^{-1}\).
3. Conductivity \(\kappa = \frac{G \cdot l}{A}\) has units \(\frac{\mathrm{S} \cdot \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}} = \mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}\).
4. Molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa}{c}\), with \(\kappa\) in \(\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}\) and \(c\) in \(\mathrm{mol\ m^{-3}}\), has SI units \(\frac{\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}}{\mathrm{mol\ m^{-3}}} = \mathrm{S\ m^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, Resistance pairs with \(\Omega\), Conductance pairs with \(\mathrm{S}\), Conductivity pairs with \(\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}\), and Molar conductivity pairs with \(\mathrm{S\ m^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q02 - Commercial cells and their electrode-electrolyte systems

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical cells/batteries in List I with their characteristic anode and electrolyte components in List II:

List I (Cell/Battery)List II (Components)
(1) Dry cell (Leclanché cell)(A) Lead anode and \(38\%\) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) solution
(2) Mercury cell(B) Zinc container anode and moist \(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}\text{–}\mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}\) paste
(3) Lead storage battery(C) Porous carbon electrodes and concentrated aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)
(4) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell(D) Zinc–mercury amalgam anode and \(\mathrm{KOH}\text{–}\mathrm{ZnO}\) paste

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary batteries, secondary batteries, and fuel cells are galvanic cells distinguished by their specific electrode materials and electrolytes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Cell
1. The dry cell (Leclanché cell) uses a zinc container as the anode, a graphite rod surrounded by \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2}\) and carbon as the cathode, and a moist paste of \(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}\) as the electrolyte.
2. The mercury cell uses a zinc–mercury amalgam as the anode, a paste of \(\mathrm{HgO}\) and carbon as the cathode, and a paste of \(\mathrm{KOH}\) and \(\mathrm{ZnO}\) as the electrolyte.
3. The lead storage battery uses a lead anode, a lead grid packed with \(\mathrm{PbO}_{2}\) as the cathode, and a \(38\%\) solution of sulphuric acid as the electrolyte.
4. The \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell bubbles hydrogen and oxygen through porous carbon electrodes into concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Dry cell matches with zinc container anode and moist \(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}\text{–}\mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}\) paste; Mercury cell matches with zinc–mercury amalgam anode and \(\mathrm{KOH}\text{–}\mathrm{ZnO}\) paste; Lead storage battery matches with lead anode and \(38\%\) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) solution; and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell matches with porous carbon electrodes and concentrated aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q03 - Standard reduction potentials of key half-cells

questiontext.text:
Match the half-cell reduction reactions in List I with their standard electrode potentials (\(E^{\ominus}\)) at \(298\text{ K}\) in List II:

List I (Half-cell Reaction)List II (\(E^{\ominus} / \text{V}\))
(1) \(\mathrm{F}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{F}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\)(A) \(0.00\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Li}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li(s)}\)(B) \(+2.87\)
(3) \(2\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\)(C) \(+0.34\)
(4) \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)(D) \(-3.05\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard electrode potentials measure the tendency of a species to undergo reduction relative to the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), which is arbitrarily assigned \(0.00\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Half-Cell
1. Fluorine gas (\(\mathrm{F}_{2}\)) is the strongest oxidising agent and has the highest standard reduction potential of \(+2.87\text{ V}\).
2. Lithium ion (\(\mathrm{Li}^{+}\)) has the lowest standard reduction potential of \(-3.05\text{ V}\), making lithium metal the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution.
3. The \(2\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_{2}\) couple is the reference electrode with \(E^{\ominus} = 0.00\text{ V}\).
4. The \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}\) couple has a positive standard reduction potential of \(+0.34\text{ V}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(\mathrm{F}_{2}/\mathrm{F}^{-}\) couple pairs with \(+2.87\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Li}^{+}/\mathrm{Li}\) pairs with \(-3.05\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_{2}\) pairs with \(0.00\text{ V}\), and \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}\) pairs with \(+0.34\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q04 - Daniell cell behaviour under external potential

questiontext.text:
Match the operating conditions of a Daniell cell (\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)) in List I with the corresponding cell behaviour in List II:

List I (Condition)List II (Cell Behaviour)
(1) \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\)(A) No flow of electrons or current; no chemical reaction
(2) \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)(B) Equilibrium attained with \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\)
(3) \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\)(C) Electrons flow from \(\mathrm{Zn}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\); \(\mathrm{Zn}\) dissolves at anode
(4) \(\Delta_{r}G = 0\) (closed circuit)(D) Electrons flow from \(\mathrm{Cu}\) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\); \(\mathrm{Zn}\) deposits at cathode

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An external opposing potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) applied to a galvanic cell modifies the net driving force for electron transfer, while \(\Delta_{r}G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}\) governs spontaneity and equilibrium.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Condition
1. When \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\), the Daniell cell continues to operate spontaneously as a galvanic cell: electrons flow from the zinc rod to the copper rod, zinc dissolves at the anode, and copper deposits at the cathode.
2. When \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), the opposing voltage exactly balances the cell potential, so no current flows and no chemical reaction occurs.
3. When \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\), the cell operates as an electrolytic cell in the reverse direction: electrons flow from copper to zinc, copper dissolves at the anode, and zinc deposits at the cathode.
4. When \(\Delta_{r}G = 0\) in a closed circuit, the reaction reaches equilibrium and \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\) corresponds to electron flow from \(\mathrm{Zn}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\); \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\) corresponds to zero current and no reaction; \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\) corresponds to electron flow from \(\mathrm{Cu}\) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\); and \(\Delta_{r}G = 0\) corresponds to equilibrium with \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q05 - Classification of materials by electrical conductivity

questiontext.text:
Match the materials/solutions in List I with their electrical conduction classification in List II:

List I (Material/Solution)List II (Classification)
(1) Silicon and Germanium(A) Semiconductor
(2) Glass and Teflon(B) Insulator
(3) \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\)(C) Ionic (electrolytic) conductor
(4) Silver and Copper(D) Electronic (metallic) conductor

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Materials are classified into conductors, semiconductors, and insulators based on the magnitude of their conductivity and whether charge is carried by electrons or ions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Material
1. Silicon and germanium have intermediate conductivities between conductors and insulators and are classified as semiconductors.
2. Glass and teflon have extremely low conductivities (\(10^{-16}\text{ to }10^{-18}\text{ S m}^{-1}\)) and are insulators.
3. Aqueous \(0.1\text{ M HCl}\) conducts electricity through the movement of \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) ions, making it an ionic (electrolytic) conductor.
4. Silver and copper are metals with very high conductivity due to electron movement, making them electronic (metallic) conductors.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Silicon and Germanium pair with Semiconductor, Glass and Teflon pair with Insulator, \(0.1\text{ M HCl(aq)}\) pairs with Ionic conductor, and Silver and Copper pair with Electronic conductor.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q06 - Electrolyte types and molar conductivity behaviour

questiontext.text:
Match the electrolytes in List I with their electrolyte type or molar conductivity behaviour in List II:

List I (Electrolyte)List II (Type / Behaviour)
(1) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)(A) 2–2 strong electrolyte
(2) \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\)(B) 1–1 strong electrolyte
(3) \(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\)(C) Weak electrolyte with steep rise in \(\Lambda_{m}\) on dilution
(4) \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\)(D) 2–1 strong electrolyte

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Strong electrolytes are classified by the charges on the cation and anion produced upon dissociation, which also determines the slope \(A\) in \(\Lambda_{m} = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\). Weak electrolytes show a steep nonlinear rise in \(\Lambda_{m}\) at low concentrations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Electrolyte
1. \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) dissociates into \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) (\(+1\)) and \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) (\(-1\)), so it is a 1–1 strong electrolyte.
2. \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\) dissociates into \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) (\(+2\)) and \(2\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) (\(-1\)), so it is a 2–1 strong electrolyte.
3. \(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\) dissociates into \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) (\(+2\)) and \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}\) (\(-2\)), so it is a 2–2 strong electrolyte.
4. Acetic acid (\(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\)) is a weak electrolyte whose degree of dissociation increases rapidly on dilution, causing a steep rise in \(\Lambda_{m}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) pairs with 1–1 strong electrolyte, \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\) pairs with 2–1 strong electrolyte, \(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\) pairs with 2–2 strong electrolyte, and \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) pairs with weak electrolyte with steep rise in \(\Lambda_{m}\) on dilution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q07 - Products of electrolysis for aqueous solutions

questiontext.text:
Match the electrolytic systems in List I with the corresponding products formed at the cathode and anode in List II:

List I (Electrolytic System)List II (Electrode Products)
(1) Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}\) with \(\mathrm{Ag}\) electrodes(A) \(\mathrm{Ag}\) at cathode; \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at anode
(2) Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes(B) \(\mathrm{Cu}\) at cathode; \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at anode
(3) Dilute \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes(C) \(\mathrm{Ag}\) at cathode; \(\mathrm{Ag}\) anode dissolves as \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\)
(4) Aqueous \(\mathrm{CuCl}_{2}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes(D) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at cathode; \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at anode

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Products of electrolysis depend on whether the electrodes are inert (\(\mathrm{Pt}\)) or reactive (\(\mathrm{Ag}\)), as well as the standard reduction potentials and overpotentials of competing ions and water.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each System
1. In aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}\) with reactive \(\mathrm{Ag}\) electrodes, \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) reduces to \(\mathrm{Ag}\) at the cathode, while the \(\mathrm{Ag}\) anode oxidises and dissolves as \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) ions.
2. In aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}\) with inert \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes, \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) reduces to \(\mathrm{Ag}\) at the cathode, and water is oxidised to \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at the anode.
3. In dilute \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes, \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) reduces to \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at the cathode, and water is oxidised to \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at the anode.
4. In aqueous \(\mathrm{CuCl}_{2}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes, \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) (\(E^{\ominus} = +0.34\text{ V}\)) reduces preferentially over \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) to deposit \(\mathrm{Cu}\) at the cathode, while \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at the anode due to oxygen overpotential.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}\) with \(\mathrm{Ag}\) electrodes yields \(\mathrm{Ag}\) at cathode and \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) dissolution at anode; aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes yields \(\mathrm{Ag}\) and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\); dilute \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes yields \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\); and aqueous \(\mathrm{CuCl}_{2}\) with \(\mathrm{Pt}\) electrodes yields \(\mathrm{Cu}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q08 - Charge in Faradays required for electrolytic reductions

questiontext.text:
Match the reduction processes in List I with the quantity of electricity (in Faradays) required per mole of the reactant ion in List II:

List I (Reduction Process)List II (Electricity Required)
(1) \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) to \(\mathrm{Al}\)(A) \(2\text{ F}\)
(2) \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\)(B) \(5\text{ F}\)
(3) \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) to \(\mathrm{Ag}\)(C) \(3\text{ F}\)
(4) \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\)(D) \(1\text{ F}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
One Faraday (\(1\text{ F}\)) is the charge carried by one mole of electrons. The electricity required to reduce \(1\text{ mol}\) of a species equals \(n\text{ F}\), where \(n\) is the number of moles of electrons gained per mole of the species.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Reduction
1. \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}\): requires \(3\text{ mol}\) of electrons, i.e., \(3\text{ F}\).
2. \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\): requires \(2\text{ mol}\) of electrons, i.e., \(2\text{ F}\).
3. \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}\): requires \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrons, i.e., \(1\text{ F}\).
4. \(\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 8\mathrm{H}^{+} + 5\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) (manganese changes from \(+7\) to \(+2\)): requires \(5\text{ mol}\) of electrons, i.e., \(5\text{ F}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}\) requires \(3\text{ F}\), \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\) requires \(2\text{ F}\), \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}\) requires \(1\text{ F}\), and \(\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) requires \(5\text{ F}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q09 - Overall discharge reactions of batteries and fuel cells

questiontext.text:
Match the galvanic cells in List I with their overall discharge reactions in List II:

List I (Cell/Battery)List II (Overall Reaction)
(1) Lead storage battery(A) \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\)
(2) Nickel–cadmium cell(B) \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO}_{2}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO}_{4}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\)
(3) Mercury cell(C) \(2\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\)
(4) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell(D) \(\mathrm{Cd(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{3}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CdO(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{2}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each commercial battery or fuel cell has a characteristic net redox reaction formed by adding its anode and cathode half-cell reactions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Cell Reaction
1. In a lead storage battery during discharge, \(\mathrm{Pb}\) and \(\mathrm{PbO}_{2}\) react with \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) to form \(\mathrm{PbSO}_{4}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\).
2. In a rechargeable nickel–cadmium cell during discharge, \(\mathrm{Cd(s)}\) reduces \(\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{3}(\mathrm{s})\) to \(\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{2}(\mathrm{s})\) while forming \(\mathrm{CdO(s)}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\).
3. In a mercury cell, \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}\) reduces \(\mathrm{HgO(s)}\) to \(\mathrm{Hg(l)}\) while forming \(\mathrm{ZnO(s)}\).
4. In a \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen combine electrochemically to produce liquid water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lead storage battery pairs with the \(\mathrm{Pb}/\mathrm{PbO}_{2}/\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) reaction, Nickel–cadmium cell pairs with the \(\mathrm{Cd}/\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{3}\) reaction, Mercury cell pairs with the \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}/\mathrm{HgO}\) reaction, and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell pairs with \(2\mathrm{H}_{2} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q10 - Electrochemical aspects and prevention of corrosion

questiontext.text:
Match the corrosion-related terms in List I with their correct chemical representations or methods in List II:

List I (Term)List II (Representation / Method)
(1) Anodic reaction in rusting of iron(A) \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\)
(2) Cathodic reaction in rusting of iron(B) Connecting to a sacrificial \(\mathrm{Mg}\) or \(\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode
(3) Chemical formula of rust(C) \(\mathrm{Fe(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\)
(4) Electrochemical prevention of corrosion(D) \(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Rusting of iron is an electrochemical phenomenon in which iron undergoes oxidation at an anodic spot and oxygen is reduced in the presence of \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions at a cathodic spot.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. At the anodic spot, iron is oxidised to ferrous ions: \(\mathrm{Fe(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\).
2. At the cathodic spot, oxygen is reduced in acidic medium: \(\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\).
3. Ferrous ions are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to ferric ions, forming rust as hydrated ferric oxide, \(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\).
4. An electrochemical method to prevent corrosion is connecting the iron object to a sacrificial electrode of a more reactive metal such as \(\mathrm{Mg}\) or \(\mathrm{Zn}\), which corrodes itself to save the object.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Anodic reaction pairs with \(\mathrm{Fe(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\), Cathodic reaction pairs with \(\mathrm{O}_{2} + 4\mathrm{H}^{+} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\), Rust formula pairs with \(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\), and Electrochemical prevention pairs with sacrificial \(\mathrm{Mg}\) or \(\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q11 - Limiting molar conductivities of individual ions

questiontext.text:
Match the aqueous ions in List I with their limiting molar conductivities \(\lambda^{\circ}\) at \(298\text{ K}\) (in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)) in List II:

List I (Ion)List II (\(\lambda^{\circ} / (\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}})\))
(1) \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\)(A) \(160.0\)
(2) \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\)(B) \(349.6\)
(3) \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}\)(C) \(40.9\)
(4) \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-}\)(D) \(199.1\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At infinite dilution, each ion migrates independently and contributes a characteristic limiting molar conductivity \(\lambda^{\circ}\) in water at \(298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Ion
From standard limiting molar conductivity data in water at \(298\text{ K}\):
1. \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) has the highest ionic conductivity: \(349.6\text{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).
2. \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\) has the next highest value: \(199.1\text{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).
3. \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}\) has \(\lambda^{\circ} = 160.0\text{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).
4. \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-}\) has \(\lambda^{\circ} = 40.9\text{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) pairs with \(349.6\), \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\) pairs with \(199.1\), \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}\) pairs with \(160.0\), and \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-}\) pairs with \(40.9\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q12 - Standard cell potentials of galvanic cell reactions

questiontext.text:
Given standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Fe}} = -0.44\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\), and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}|\mathrm{O}_{2}|\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}} = +1.23\text{ V}\). Match the cell reactions in List I with their standard cell potentials \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) in List II:

List I (Cell Reaction)List II (\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\))
(1) \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)(A) \(0.46\text{ V}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\)(B) \(1.67\text{ V}\)
(3) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Ag(s)}\)(C) \(1.10\text{ V}\)
(4) \(2\mathrm{Fe(s)} + \mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\)(D) \(0.03\text{ V}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potentials: \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn} = -0.76\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Fe} = -0.44\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu} = +0.34\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} = +0.77\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag} = +0.80\text{ V}\), and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}/\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} = +1.23\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For every galvanic cell reaction, the species being reduced is the cathode and the species being oxidised is the anode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{anode}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + \mathrm{Cu}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\text{ V}\).
2. For \(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.80 - 0.34 = 0.46\text{ V}\).
3. For \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + \mathrm{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + \mathrm{Ag}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.80 - 0.77 = 0.03\text{ V}\).
4. For \(2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{O}_{2} + 4\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.23 - (-0.44) = 1.67\text{ V}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four calculated \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) values are positive, indicating spontaneous reactions under standard conditions. The pairings are: \(\mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) with \(1.10\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Cu}/\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) with \(0.46\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) with \(0.03\text{ V}\), and \(\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{O}_{2}\) with \(1.67\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q13 - Limiting molar conductivities of electrolytes via Kohlrausch law

questiontext.text:
Using \(\lambda^{\circ}\) values (in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)) at \(298\text{ K}\): \(\mathrm{H}^{+} = 349.6\), \(\mathrm{Na}^{+} = 50.1\), \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+} = 119.0\), \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} = 106.0\), \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-} = 76.3\), \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-} = 40.9\), and \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-} = 160.0\), match the electrolytes in List I with their \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) values in List II:

List I (Electrolyte)List II (\(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ} / (\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}})\))
(1) \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\)(A) \(126.4\)
(2) \(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\)(B) \(271.6\)
(3) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)(C) \(390.5\)
(4) \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\)(D) \(266.0\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Ionic limiting molar conductivities at \(298 ext{ K}\) (in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)): \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} = 349.6\), \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na}^{+}} = 50.1\), \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}} = 119.0\), \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}} = 106.0\), \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl}^{-}} = 76.3\), \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-}} = 40.9\), and \(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}} = 160.0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At infinite dilution, electrolytes are completely dissociated and ions migrate independently without interionic interference.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions:
\[\Lambda_{m}^{\circ} = u_{+}\lambda_{+}^{\circ} + u_{-}\lambda_{-}^{\circ}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}} + 2\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl}^{-}} = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 119.0 + 152.6 = 271.6 ext{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).
2. \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}} = 106.0 + 160.0 = 266.0 ext{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).
3. \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl}^{-}} = 50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4 ext{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).
4. \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-}} = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5 ext{ S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All stoichiometric coefficients \( u_{+}\) and \( u_{-}\) are properly accounted for, especially \(2\) for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) in \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\). Thus, \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\) pairs with \(271.6\), \(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\) pairs with \(266.0\), \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) pairs with \(126.4\), and \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\) pairs with \(390.5\).

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical concepts in List I with their corresponding mathematical equations at \(298\text{ K}\) in List II:

List I (Concept)List II (Equation)
(1) Nernst equation for cell emf(A) \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\)
(2) Equilibrium constant from \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\)(B) \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K_{c}\)
(3) Standard Gibbs energy from \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\)(C) \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -RT\ln K_{c}\)
(4) Standard Gibbs energy from \(K_{c}\)(D) \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Nernst equation relates cell potential to reaction quotient \(Q\), and at equilibrium (\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0, Q = K_{c}\)) connects \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) to both \(K_{c}\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Relation
1. At \(298\text{ K}\), \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\), so the Nernst equation is \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q\).
2. Setting \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\) and \(Q = K_{c}\) gives \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K_{c}\).
3. Maximum reversible electrical work equals the decrease in Gibbs energy: \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\).
4. Combining with the thermodynamic identity yields \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -RT\ln K_{c}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nernst equation pairs with \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q\), Equilibrium constant relation pairs with \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K_{c}\), Standard Gibbs energy from \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) pairs with \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\), and Standard Gibbs energy from \(K_{c}\) pairs with \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -RT\ln K_{c}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q15 - Quantitative electricity required in electrolytic processes

questiontext.text:
Match the electrolytic processes in List I with the quantity of electricity required in List II (take atomic masses \(\mathrm{Ca} = 40\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Al} = 27\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), and \(1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\)):

List I (Electrolytic Process)List II (Quantity of Electricity)
(1) Produce \(20.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{Ca}\) from molten \(\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}\)(A) \(4.44\text{ F}\)
(2) Produce \(40.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{Al}\) from molten \(\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\)(B) \(96500\text{ C}\)
(3) Oxidise \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) to \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\)(C) \(1\text{ F}\)
(4) Oxidise \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\)(D) \(193000\text{ C}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molar masses: \(\mathrm{Ca} = 40\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Al} = 27\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), and \(1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume \(100\%\) current efficiency for all four electrolytic processes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Moles of substance \(= \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}\), and charge required \(Q = n_{\text{substance}} \times z\text{ F}\), where \(z\) is the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For \(20.0\text{ g}\) \(\mathrm{Ca}\): \(\text{moles of Ca} = \frac{20.0}{40} = 0.5\text{ mol}\). Since \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca}\), charge \(= 0.5 \times 2\text{ F} = 1\text{ F}\).
2. For \(40.0\text{ g}\) \(\mathrm{Al}\): \(\text{moles of Al} = \frac{40.0}{27}\text{ mol}\). Since \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}\), charge \(= \frac{40.0}{27} \times 3\text{ F} = \frac{40}{9}\text{ F} \approx 4.44\text{ F}\).
3. For oxidising \(1\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) to \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\): \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2} + 2\mathrm{H}^{+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-}\), so charge \(= 2\text{ F} = 2 \times 96500\text{ C} = 193000\text{ C}\).
4. For oxidising \(1\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{FeO}\) (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)) to \(\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\) (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)): \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + \mathrm{e}^{-}\), so charge \(= 1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each stoichiometric electron count matches the calculated Faradays or Coulombs. Thus, \(20.0\text{ g}\) \(\mathrm{Ca}\) pairs with \(1\text{ F}\), \(40.0\text{ g}\) \(\mathrm{Al}\) pairs with \(4.44\text{ F}\), \(1\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_{2}\) pairs with \(193000\text{ C}\), and \(1\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{FeO} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}\) pairs with \(96500\text{ C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCH_Q16 - Cell constant, conductivity, and molar conductivity calculations

questiontext.text:
Match the experimental data for aqueous \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solutions in a conductivity cell at \(298\text{ K}\) in List I with the corresponding calculated values in List II:

List I (Experimental Data)List II (Calculated Value)
(1) \(R = 100\text{ }\Omega\), \(\kappa = 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\)(A) \(\Lambda_{m} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
(2) \(G^{*} = 129\text{ m}^{-1}\), \(R = 520\text{ }\Omega\)(B) \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\)
(3) \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\), \(c = 20\text{ mol m}^{-3}\)(C) \(G^{*} = 0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\)
(4) \(\kappa = 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\), \(R = 1500\text{ }\Omega\)(D) \(G^{*} = 129\text{ m}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four sets of experimental measurements of resistance \(R\), conductivity \(\kappa\), cell constant \(G^{*}\), and concentration \(c\) for aqueous \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solutions at \(298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All units are kept consistent within each pair (SI units \(\mathrm{m}\), \(\mathrm{S m}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{mol m}^{-3}\) for the first three pairs, and CGS units \(\mathrm{cm}\), \(\mathrm{S cm}^{-1}\) for the fourth pair).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Cell constant: \(G^{*} = R \cdot \kappa\)
Conductivity: \(\kappa = \frac{G^{*}}{R}\)
Molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa}{c}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(G^{*} = R \cdot \kappa = 100\text{ }\Omega \times 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1} = 129\text{ m}^{-1}\).
2. \(\kappa = \frac{G^{*}}{R} = \frac{129\text{ m}^{-1}}{520\text{ }\Omega} = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\).
3. \(\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa}{c} = \frac{0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}}{20\text{ mol m}^{-3}} = 0.0124\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
4. \(G^{*} = R \cdot \kappa = 1500\text{ }\Omega \times 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1} = 0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four calculations are dimensionally consistent. Thus, \(R = 100\text{ }\Omega, \kappa = 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\) pairs with \(G^{*} = 129\text{ m}^{-1}\); \(G^{*} = 129\text{ m}^{-1}, R = 520\text{ }\Omega\) pairs with \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\); \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}, c = 20\text{ mol m}^{-3}\) pairs with \(\Lambda_{m} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\); and \(\kappa = 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}, R = 1500\text{ }\Omega\) pairs with \(G^{*} = 0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\).
